screens.title: The Proxy Pattern: Controlling Access to Objects
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the Proxy pattern, a structural pattern that gives you a controllable stand-in for another object. You will learn why a proxy exists, how it preserves the same interface as the real subject, and the common roles proxies play: deferring expensive creation, applying permission checks, representing remote resources, or performing additional bookkeeping when an object is accessed. We'll anchor these ideas with concrete Java examples: a virtual proxy that delays loading large images until they are actually displayed, and a protection proxy that enforces a simple authorization rule before allowing access to sensitive data. As you learn, notice a repeated contract: the proxy and the real subject implement the same interface so clients remain unaware of the substitution. That property makes proxies easy to introduce but also easy to misuse when indirection brings unnecessary complexity. By the end of this chapter you'll know how and when to implement a proxy in Java, common pitfalls to avoid, and how the proxy's intent differs from patterns like the Decorator. Think about a place in your code where creation or access costs are high — could a proxy help?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A proxy is a stand-in that implements the same interface as a real object and adds control logic—lazy creation, access checks, remote access, or bookkeeping—before delegating to the real subject.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Introduction
The Proxy Pattern
A surrogate that controls access, creation, or representation of a real object.
Virtual
Defer creation of expensive objects until needed.
Protection
Enforce permission checks before delegating.
Remote
Represent objects in a different address space.
When to use

You need control over access or expensive creation, or you must represent a remote resource without changing client code.

Common mistake

Using a proxy where a simple direct call or wrapper suffices adds unnecessary indirection and maintenance cost.

Proxy and Real Subject implement the same interface so clients are unaware of substitution.

screens.title: What is a Proxy?
screens.narratorSegment: A proxy is a structural pattern that provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access. In practical terms, the proxy implements the same subject interface as the real object so client code can call methods as before, while the proxy performs additional responsibilities such as access checks, lazy initialization, network marshalling, or bookkeeping. Think of a proxy as a receptionist who answers calls for an executive. The receptionist can screen callers, schedule meetings, or pass on messages only when necessary. This preserves the executive’s availability while adding control. A concrete example: an Image proxy stands in for a large image file. The proxy is lightweight and only creates and loads the heavy RealImage when a display request occurs, saving memory and startup time. A common misconception is to confuse wrapping for decoration — Decorator focuses on adding behavior, while Proxy focuses on controlling access and timing. Always ensure your proxy preserves the observable behavior of the real subject and handles exceptions safely. Would your current design benefit from postponing creation or adding a safety gate? What is a Proxy? means proxy = surrogate that implements the same interface to control access, defer creation, or represent remote objects without changing client code.. In practical terms, a precise definition and everyday metaphor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › What is a Proxy?
Proxy explained
A surrogate that controls access, timing, or representation while preserving the Subject interface.
Key claim
The proxy and real subject implement the same interface so the client is unaware of the substitution.
Metaphor
A receptionist screens and forwards requests for an executive, adding control and delay when needed.
Misconception
Proxy is not a Decorator. Decorator adds features; Proxy manages when and whether a feature is reached.
Key Takeaway

Use a proxy when you need to control access, defer creation, or represent a remote resource while keeping client interactions unchanged.

Concrete example
Virtual proxy for large images.
// Subject interface
public interface Image {
  void display();
}

// RealSubject: expensive to create
public class RealImage implements Image {
  private String filename;

  public RealImage(String filename) {
    this.filename = filename;
    loadImageFromDisk();
  }

  private void loadImageFromDisk() {
    System.out.println("Loading " + filename + " from disk...");
    try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    System.out.println(filename + " loaded.");
  }

  public void display() {
    System.out.println("Displaying " + filename);
  }
}

screens.title: Proxy Structure and Roles
screens.narratorSegment: To implement a proxy correctly you must understand the three roles: the Subject interface, the Real Subject that performs the actual work, and the Proxy that implements the Subject and forwards requests. The Subject defines the contract both sides obey. The Real Subject contains business logic and possibly expensive initialization. The Proxy holds a reference to the Real Subject and may create it lazily, check permissions, or marshal calls to a remote object. A concrete design property is that the client depends only on the Subject type; it never needs to know whether it received a proxy or the real subject. One common trap is exposing the proxy’s internal reference or specific type — doing so breaks the abstraction and couples clients to the proxy. Another important point: the proxy must mimic the real subject’s observable behavior, including exception semantics, otherwise tests and callers will see different outcomes. Consider adding robust exception translation and careful lifecycle management in the proxy. To check your understanding, ask whether the proxy can safely delay construction or must instantiate immediately for correctness. Proxy Structure and Roles means three roles — subject, real subject, proxy — each with a clear responsibility: contract, implementation, and access control/delegation respectively.. In practical terms, subject, real subject, and proxy — the anatomy of substitution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Proxy Structure
Roles
Each role has distinct responsibilities that keep clients decoupled from implementation details.
Subject
Defines the methods both proxy and real subject expose. Clients compile to this type.
Real Subject
Performs actual work and may be expensive to create or located remotely.
Proxy
Implements Subject, holds reference to Real Subject, and applies control logic before delegating.
Pro Tip
Keep the proxy’s public surface identical to the subject and avoid leaking proxy-specific methods to clients.
UML-style cards
Subject
interface Image { void display(); }
Real Subject
RealImage implements heavy loading and display behavior.
Proxy
ImageProxy implements the same interface and controls when RealImage is created and used.
Check your understanding

Can a proxy change return values? No — it should preserve observable behavior; only control logic and timing should differ.

screens.title: Virtual Proxy: RealImage Code
screens.narratorSegment: Before building the proxy, inspect the real subject to see why lazy initialization helps. The RealImage class models an expensive resource: construction triggers a load operation that simulates disk or network latency. In a GUI or server application, creating many RealImage instances at startup can hurt responsiveness and increase memory pressure. The code shows a constructor that calls a private load method and a display method that only prints when the image is ready. The key observation is that the expensive operation is tied to object creation, not method invocation. That gives us a clear strategy: let the proxy postpone constructing RealImage until display is actually required. A practical pitfall to watch for is side effects in the real subject's constructor. If construction registers global state or opens resources, delaying construction changes the application’s timing and may affect behavior. Confirm side-effect-free construction or adjust accordingly when writing a proxy. Virtual Proxy: RealImage Code means realimage performs costly initialization during construction; detecting that cost is the reason to introduce a virtual proxy that defers instantiation until needed.. In practical terms, why realimage is expensive and how it behaves at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › RealImage Walkthrough
RealImage — expensive creation
Inspect the code that performs costly loading in the constructor.
// Real Subject: Expensive to load
public class RealImage implements Image {
  private String filename;

  public RealImage(String filename) {
    this.filename = filename;
    loadImageFromDisk(); // Expensive operation during construction
  }

  private void loadImageFromDisk() {
    System.out.println("Loading " + filename + " from disk...");
    try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    System.out.println(filename + " loaded.");
  }

  @Override
  public void display() {
    System.out.println("Displaying " + filename);
  }
}
Runtime observation
Creating RealImage triggers loadImageFromDisk which simulates delay. If many images are created eagerly, startup is slow.
Design note
If the constructor has side effects beyond loading, delaying creation may change behavior. Audit those effects before deferring instantiation.
Key Takeaway

Lazy initialization moves cost from creation time to first use. Use it when many objects may never be used.

screens.title: ImageProxy Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: The ImageProxy demonstrates a simple virtual proxy: it stores the filename and a nullable reference to the RealImage. The display method checks whether the real reference is null and only then constructs the RealImage, invoking its expensive load. After construction, the proxy delegates display calls to the real subject. This approach ensures the expensive load happens at most once per proxied image. Important implementation concerns include thread safety, null checks, and preserving exception behavior. In multi-threaded contexts you may need to synchronize the lazy initialization so two threads don't create two RealImage instances. Also, the proxy should propagate exceptions from the real subject to callers rather than swallowing them. The proxy pattern is intentionally simple here, but you can extend it to include caching, access logging, or reference counting. When you implement, test both first-call and subsequent-call behavior to confirm lazy init and correct delegation. ImageProxy Implementation means proxy checks for a null real reference, constructs the real subject on demand, and delegates calls thereafter; handle thread safety and exception propagation carefully.. In practical terms, how the proxy defers realimage construction and delegates display. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › ImageProxy
ImageProxy — lazy initialization
The proxy holds the filename and a reference to RealImage, creating it on first use.
// Proxy: Controls access and provides lazy loading
public class ImageProxy implements Image {
  private String filename;
  private RealImage realImage; // Reference to the real subject

  public ImageProxy(String filename) {
    this.filename = filename;
  }

  @Override
  public void display() {
    if (realImage == null) {
      // Lazy initialization
      realImage = new RealImage(filename);
    }
    realImage.display(); // Delegate to the real subject
  }
}
Safety note
Consider synchronization for multithreaded environments and ensure exceptions from RealImage surface to callers.
Example scenario
A gallery app creates proxies for each image at startup; thumbnails show immediately while full images load when viewed.
Key Takeaway

A virtual proxy delays expensive work until necessary; verify thread-safety and exception semantics in your implementation.

screens.title: Using Proxies: Client Code and Output
screens.narratorSegment: The client code provides the most convincing proof that the virtual proxy works. In a simple ImageViewer, the application creates proxies for each filename but does not construct RealImage objects. Only when a proxy’s display method is invoked does the RealImage appear, print loading messages, and then display the image. Subsequent display calls on the same proxy do not reload the image because the RealImage reference is already set. This demonstrates both lazy initialization and caching of the instantiated object. In practice, such behavior improves responsiveness and reduces memory usage when many potential objects are rarely accessed. A common debugging step is to print messages from the proxy and real subject to validate when instantiation occurs. The key checks for your code are: proxies are cheap to create, the first display triggers creation, subsequent displays reuse the same real instance, and denied or exceptional paths propagate readable messages to the caller. Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Client Example
Client: ImageViewer
Create proxies early, trigger real loads only on display.
// Client code
public class ImageViewer {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println("Application starting...");

    Image image1 = new ImageProxy("photo1.jpg");
    Image image2 = new ImageProxy("report_chart.png");

    System.out.println("Proxies created. Real images not loaded until display is called.");

    System.out.println("
--- Displaying image1 ---");
    image1.display(); // Loads photo1.jpg

    System.out.println("
--- Displaying image1 again ---");
    image1.display(); // Just displays photo1.jpg

    System.out.println("
--- Displaying image2 ---");
    image2.display(); // Loads report_chart.png
  }
}
Simulated runtime output
Application starting... Proxies created. Real images not loaded until display is called. --- Displaying image1 --- Loading photo1.jpg from disk... photo1.jpg loaded. Displaying photo1.jpg --- Displaying image1 again --- Displaying photo1.jpg --- Displaying image2 --- Loading report_chart.png from disk... report_chart.png loaded. Displaying report_chart.png
Reflection
If you see loading messages only at first display, the proxy is behaving as intended. If loading occurs at proxy creation, the proxy is not lazy.

screens.title: Protection Proxy: Guarding Sensitive Operations
screens.narratorSegment: A protection proxy controls access to a real subject based on permissions or roles. The chapter gives a hands-on starter example: a SensitiveDataService that fetches confidential information and a SensitiveDataServiceProxy that checks authorization before delegating. The proxy checks the caller’s identity or role and either constructs the real service lazily and forwards the request, or returns an access denied response. This pattern is valuable when you must ensure only authorized clients can invoke sensitive operations. When implementing a protection proxy, avoid performing complex authentication in-line; instead call a dedicated security service if available. Also, be careful about error messages — do not leak sensitive information in denial responses. In testing, verify three scenarios: an authorized user receives the data, an unauthorized user receives a denial, and the proxy initializes the real service only when authorization succeeds. This demonstrates both access control and lazy initialization in a single proxy. Protection Proxy: Guarding Sensitive Operations means a protection proxy checks permissions before allowing operations and can also lazily initialize the real service to avoid unnecessary costs for unauthorized callers.. In practical terms, add authorization checks and lazy initialization to protect a sensitive service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A protection proxy checks permissions before allowing operations and can also lazily initialize the real service to avoid unnecessary costs for unauthorized callers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Protection Proxy
Starter code
Proxy adds authorization check before delegating to the real service.
// Proxy skeleton from chapter
class SensitiveDataServiceProxy implements DataService {
  private SensitiveDataService realService;
  private String authorizedUserRole; // e.g., "ADMIN"

  public SensitiveDataServiceProxy(String authorizedUserRole) {
    this.authorizedUserRole = authorizedUserRole;
  }

  private boolean checkAuthorization(String userId) {
    System.out.println("Proxy: Checking authorization for user: " + userId);
    return userId.equals(authorizedUserRole); // Simplified example
  }

  @Override
  public String fetchData(String userId) {
    if (checkAuthorization(userId)) {
      if (realService == null) { realService = new SensitiveDataService(); }
      return realService.fetchData(userId);
    } else {
      System.out.println("Proxy: Access Denied for user: " + userId + ". Insufficient privileges.");
      return "Access Denied";
    }
  }
}
Testing checklist
  • Authorized user receives confidential data.
  • Unauthorized user receives a denial message without leaked details.
  • Real service is constructed only when access is allowed.
Security note
Do not conflate authorization checks with auditing. Authorization denies access; auditing records who attempted access. Keep them separate when needed.
Key Takeaway

A protection proxy should enforce access policy and avoid performing expensive work for unauthorized callers by delaying real service creation until authorization succeeds.

screens.title: Remote & Smart Reference Proxies
screens.narratorSegment: Two additional proxy variants appear commonly: remote proxies and smart reference proxies. A remote proxy provides a local representation for an object that lives in another address space. It is responsible for marshalling calls, encoding arguments, sending requests across the network, and decoding results. Although the chapter mentions Java RMI as an example, the important lesson is that remote proxies abstract network details so clients call remote services as if they were local. A smart reference proxy performs auxiliary actions when the real subject is accessed: it may count references, acquire locks, or pre-load state. For instance, a smart reference could increment a usage counter whenever the object is accessed to support eviction or metrics. Both variants share the same interface property and the same responsibility to preserve observable behavior. When using remote proxies, consider network reliability and error handling carefully; for smart references, take care not to introduce side effects that change business semantics unintentionally. Remote & Smart Reference Proxies means remote proxies hide network details for a remote subject; smart reference proxies add bookkeeping behavior like reference counting or locking when the subject is accessed.. In practical terms, representing remote objects and adding bookkeeping on access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Remote Proxy
Represents an object in a different address space. It marshals calls and handles network errors so the client can use the remote service transparently.
Consideration
Network failures and latency are now part of the proxy’s responsibilities. Ensure robust error handling and retries where appropriate.
Smart Reference Proxy

Example
Increment a usage counter each time display is called to support eviction policies.
Misuse warning

screens.title: Proxy vs Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: Proxy and Decorator both wrap another object and often share the same interface, which leads to confusion. The decisive difference is intent. A Decorator adds responsibilities or behavior to an object dynamically — for example, adding logging or formatting output — without changing when the underlying object is accessed. The Proxy’s goal is access control or indirection: it manages when or whether the real subject is reached or how the call is transported. In practice, examine why the wrapper exists. If the wrapper’s duty is to change the object’s observable features, it’s a Decorator. If the wrapper’s duty is to gate or delay access, marshal calls, or perform bookkeeping on access, it’s a Proxy. A concrete contrast: adding caching behavior to speed up responses is often a Decorator, while deferring expensive creation until first use is a virtual Proxy. Mislabeling can lead to poor design decisions; use the pattern that fits the intent, not the surface structure. Proxy vs Decorator means both patterns wrap objects, but decorator enhances behavior while proxy controls access or timing; choose by intent, not by appearance.. In practical terms, same wrapping form, different intent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Safety Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Proxies add indirection, and with indirection come pitfalls. First, unnecessary proxies increase complexity and can degrade performance if the proxy performs heavy work on every access. Second, incorrect lazy initialization exposes race conditions in multithreaded environments; if two threads create separate real instances you lose the benefit and create subtle bugs. Third, a proxy that swallows exceptions or changes error semantics will surprise clients and break contracts. Fourth, careless protection proxies can leak sensitive information in denial messages or perform authorization checks inconsistently. Lastly, remote proxies must cope with network unreliability and latency; they should translate network errors into meaningful application-level exceptions or retries. To mitigate these risks, measure the actual cost you avoid, test concurrency paths, preserve exception semantics, centralize security checks when possible, and document the proxy’s lifecycle and side effects. A quick checklist helps: do you need indirection, does lazy init keep semantics, are failures handled clearly, and have you considered threading? Common Pitfalls and Safety Considerations means avoid unnecessary indirection, preserve semantics, handle concurrency and exceptions, and ensure protection proxies do not leak sensitive information.. In practical terms, when a proxy can hurt more than help. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Pitfalls checklist
Common mistakes to avoid when using proxies.
Unnecessary indirection
Only add a proxy when it reduces cost or increases safety; otherwise keep design simple.
Thread safety
Use synchronization or double-checked locking for lazy init in multithreaded contexts.
Exception handling
Propagate exceptions from the real subject rather than hiding them to preserve client expectations.
Security leaks
Do not reveal details in access denied messages; keep responses minimal.
Network reliability
Remote proxies must map network errors to application-level behavior thoughtfully.
Testing
Write tests for first access, repeated access, denied access, and concurrent access paths.
Quick decision guide

If the indirection reduces real cost or enforces essential safety checks, a proxy is justified; otherwise prefer direct access.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the Proxy pattern, a structural pattern that gives you a controllable stand-in for another object. You will learn why a proxy exists, how it preserves the same interface as the real subject, and the common roles proxies play: deferring expensive creation, applying permission checks, representing remote resources, or performing additional bookkeeping when an object is accessed. We'll anchor these ideas with concrete Java examples: a virtual proxy that delays loading large images until they are actually displayed, and a protection proxy that enforces a simple authorization rule before allowing access to sensitive data. As you learn, notice a repeated contract: the proxy and the real subject implement the same interface so clients remain unaware of the substitution. That property makes proxies easy to introduce but also easy to misuse when indirection brings unnecessary complexity. By the end of this chapter you'll know how and when to implement a proxy in Java, common pitfalls to avoid, and how the proxy's intent differs from patterns like the Decorator. Think about a place in your code where creation or access costs are high — could a proxy help?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define the Proxy pattern, recognize its purpose, and implement common proxy variants in Java. You will distinguish remote, virtual, protection, and smart-reference proxies by their intent and typical responsibilities. Practically, you will implement a virtual proxy to defer expensive object creation and a protection proxy to add an authorization check around a sensitive service. You will also learn to identify scenarios where introducing a proxy improves resource use or security, and where it would be unnecessary overhead. For each objective you will see a brief example, a mnemonic to help recall the intent, and a milestone that indicates verified competency. These objectives prepare you to read and reason about proxy code in frameworks like lazy-loading ORMs and dynamic proxies used for concerns like security or transactions.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical outcomes. You will implement and test a virtual proxy that defers loading large resources, verifying that the real object is not created until invoked. You will also implement a protection proxy to apply a simple authorization check around a sensitive service and observe different client behaviors for authorized and unauthorized callers. These exercises teach you subtle requirements: the proxy must preserve the Subject interface, handle exceptions from the real subject safely, and avoid leaking internal state. The hands-on activity in this chapter gives starter code with TODO markers so you can add the proxy logic and test three client scenarios. Finally, you will be able to answer conceptual assessment questions: identify the most suitable proxy type for a scenario and explain the difference in intent between Proxy and Decorator. These skills make you ready to use proxies in frameworks that rely on dynamic proxies or lazy loading.

A proxy is a structural pattern that provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access. In practical terms, the proxy implements the same subject interface as the real object so client code can call methods as before, while the proxy performs additional responsibilities such as access checks, lazy initialization, network marshalling, or bookkeeping. Think of a proxy as a receptionist who answers calls for an executive. The receptionist can screen callers, schedule meetings, or pass on messages only when necessary. This preserves the executive’s availability while adding control. A concrete example: an Image proxy stands in for a large image file. The proxy is lightweight and only creates and loads the heavy RealImage when a display request occurs, saving memory and startup time. A common misconception is to confuse wrapping for decoration — Decorator focuses on adding behavior, while Proxy focuses on controlling access and timing. Always ensure your proxy preserves the observable behavior of the real subject and handles exceptions safely. Would your current design benefit from postponing creation or adding a safety gate? What is a Proxy? means proxy = surrogate that implements the same interface to control access, defer creation, or represent remote objects without changing client code.. In practical terms, a precise definition and everyday metaphor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To implement a proxy correctly you must understand the three roles: the Subject interface, the Real Subject that performs the actual work, and the Proxy that implements the Subject and forwards requests. The Subject defines the contract both sides obey. The Real Subject contains business logic and possibly expensive initialization. The Proxy holds a reference to the Real Subject and may create it lazily, check permissions, or marshal calls to a remote object. A concrete design property is that the client depends only on the Subject type; it never needs to know whether it received a proxy or the real subject. One common trap is exposing the proxy’s internal reference or specific type — doing so breaks the abstraction and couples clients to the proxy. Another important point: the proxy must mimic the real subject’s observable behavior, including exception semantics, otherwise tests and callers will see different outcomes. Consider adding robust exception translation and careful lifecycle management in the proxy. To check your understanding, ask whether the proxy can safely delay construction or must instantiate immediately for correctness. Proxy Structure and Roles means three roles — subject, real subject, proxy — each with a clear responsibility: contract, implementation, and access control/delegation respectively.. In practical terms, subject, real subject, and proxy — the anatomy of substitution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before building the proxy, inspect the real subject to see why lazy initialization helps. The RealImage class models an expensive resource: construction triggers a load operation that simulates disk or network latency. In a GUI or server application, creating many RealImage instances at startup can hurt responsiveness and increase memory pressure. The code shows a constructor that calls a private load method and a display method that only prints when the image is ready. The key observation is that the expensive operation is tied to object creation, not method invocation. That gives us a clear strategy: let the proxy postpone constructing RealImage until display is actually required. A practical pitfall to watch for is side effects in the real subject's constructor. A protection proxy controls access to a real subject based on permissions or roles. Two additional proxy variants appear commonly: remote proxies and smart reference proxies. A remote proxy provides a local representation for an object that lives in another address space. It is responsible for marshalling calls, encoding arguments, sending requests across the network, and decoding results. Although the chapter mentions Java RMI as an example, the important lesson is that remote proxies abstract network details so clients call remote services as if they were local. A smart reference proxy performs auxiliary actions when the real subject is accessed: it may count references, acquire locks, or pre-load state. For instance, a smart reference could increment a usage counter whenever the object is accessed to support eviction or metrics. Both variants share the same interface property and the same responsibility to preserve observable behavior. When using remote proxies, consider network reliability and error handling carefully; for smart references, take care not to introduce side effects that change business semantics unintentionally. Proxy and Decorator both wrap another object and often share the same interface, which leads to confusion. The decisive difference is intent. A Decorator adds responsibilities or behavior to an object dynamically — for example, adding logging or formatting output — without changing when the underlying object is accessed. The Proxy’s goal is access control or indirection: it manages when or whether the real subject is reached or how the call is transported. In practice, examine why the wrapper exists. If the wrapper’s duty is to change the object’s observable features, it’s a Decorator. If the wrapper’s duty is to gate or delay access, marshal calls, or perform bookkeeping on access, it’s a Proxy. A concrete contrast: adding caching behavior to speed up responses is often a Decorator, while deferring expensive creation until first use is a virtual Proxy. Mislabeling can lead to poor design decisions; use the pattern that fits the intent, not the surface structure. Proxies add indirection, and with indirection come pitfalls. First, unnecessary proxies increase complexity and can degrade performance if the proxy performs heavy work on every access. Second, incorrect lazy initialization exposes race conditions in multithreaded environments; if two threads create separate real instances you lose the benefit and create subtle bugs. Third, a proxy that swallows exceptions or changes error semantics will surprise clients and break contracts. Fourth, careless protection proxies can leak sensitive information in denial messages or perform authorization checks inconsistently. Lastly, remote proxies must cope with network unreliability and latency; they should translate network errors into meaningful application-level exceptions or retries. To mitigate these risks, measure the actual cost you avoid, test concurrency paths, preserve exception semantics, centralize security checks when possible, and document the proxy’s lifecycle and side effects. A quick checklist helps: do you need indirection, does lazy init keep semantics, are failures handled clearly, and have you considered threading? Review the essential ideas you should remember. The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate that implements the same interface as the real subject to control access, defer creation, or represent remote objects. Virtual proxies delay expensive initialization until the object is actually needed. Protection proxies enforce authorization before allowing operations and can also defer service creation for unauthorized callers. Remote proxies hide network details so clients treat remote objects as local. Smart reference proxies perform auxiliary tasks on access such as reference counting or locking. Finally, always choose a proxy for intent: if your goal is access control or timing, use Proxy; if your goal is to add behavior, consider Decorator instead. Keep exception semantics and thread safety in mind when implementing proxies.
